title: Rolling
description: A green-bladed SANYO senpuki in a dim tatami room, seen through a phone camera's rolling shutter. The sensor reads its rows top to bottom over a thirtieth of a second, so every row catches the blades at a later moment than the row above it, and catches the room's fluorescent lamp, which pulses at 120 Hz off the same mains as the motor, at a different point in its flicker: four bands of cool light and warm shade lie across the frame and across the torn blades, the readout made visible. Left alone the fan runs on its high notch at 2395 rpm, a turn and a third per readout, so its blades, the photo's own green acrylic with its grain, dust and gloss, are read more than once down the frame: two stay hooked to the hub and trail long tapering tails, and one is torn clean off into pieces that float free of it, their texture sheared into streaks along the rows. The fan sits just off a wagon-wheel lock, so the whole torn pattern crawls slowly backwards against the 30 fps frame rate while the bands creep up. Drag up to overdrive it; drag down and it coasts through softer hooks and the wagon-wheel speeds. Let go and it returns to its notch. And the phone is held in a hand: the same readout acts on the whole picture, so even at rest the hand's faint tremor leaves the guard a slight wobble that changes every frame. Drag sideways to grab the picture and flick it: the phone swings on the hand's spring, overshoots and rings out, and while it moves every row looks from a different place, so the guard's rim leans into a parallelogram, the wires bend while it slows, the stand's legs slant, and the blades tear further or knit back as the pan adds to or takes from their sweep down the frame.
intent: The CMOS rolling shutter (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_shutter), the process behind every phone video of a propeller or a fan, after herb's generative reference 2 (a real photo pulled apart by a real process while the rest of the picture stays intact). The process is a real rolling-shutter capture. A simulated sensor runs at 29.97 fps with a 1/30 s readout and a 1/4000 s exposure per row. Row s of the frame that starts at t0 is exposed over [t0 + s * readout, + exposure] and integrated in linear light over sixteen sub-samples, so the tip smear (about 45 device px at 3590 rpm) is a ramp, not a stack of copies. The room is lit by a ring fluorescent on the same 60 Hz mains as the motor: on an old choke ballast its arc goes out every half cycle while the mains voltage is below 0.55 of its peak and re-strikes after, so its light is a 120 Hz train of bright crests and broad dark gaps (an old tube on a tired ballast re-strikes late, at 0.8 of the mains peak, so it is dark for nearly half of every cycle; the arc's light, saturating with current, goes as the 0.35 power of the voltage above re-strike). Each phosphor holds it for its own decay time (red 1.6 ms, green 1.1 ms, blue 0.4 ms, a first-order lag applied to each of ten harmonics, plus 54 to 57% of steady light per channel, the phosphors' afterglow and the daylight through the shoji), so blue drops furthest in the gap while red holds on: each gap is a broad warm plateau at about 0.56 of the mean light, which on the screen is about a quarter darker than the mean, and each crest runs cool at about 1.6 times it, plain bands across the torn blades and the guard without drowning the guard's chrome or the hub. Every row integrates the lamp over its own exposure window (each sub-sample lit at its own instant; the plate and guard by its exact mean over the window), so the 1/30 s readout spans exactly four lamp cycles and the frame carries four bright and dark bands along the sensor's rows. They are the readout itself in the picture's own light, not an overlay: they light the plate, the acrylic and the guard through the same linear composite, they turn when the readout direction turns, they shift and wash out as the exposure lengthens (?exp=N for 1/N s; at 1/120 s they vanish, and the blades blur long before that), and since 120 Hz gains 0.004 of a cycle on every 1/29.97 s frame they creep slowly up the frame, about one band every eight seconds, while the torn blades creep backwards. For each sub-sample the rotor is drawn at its angle at that exact instant, read from the rotor's own simulated history at 1/960 s steps, so a fan that speeds up or slows down during a readout shows it at the bottom of the frame. There is no warp. The curls, the floating segments and the wagon-wheel stillness (3 blades x rpm/60 = a multiple of 29.97 Hz, so 599.4, 1198.8 ... 3596.4 rpm) all come from when each row looked. The fan is an induction motor with a set speed (it can push but never brake), quadratic air drag and viscous and dry bearing friction. Left alone it runs on its high notch, a two-pole shaded-pole motor slipping a third below its 3600 rpm synchronous speed under the blades' load, at 2395 rpm. The resting speed is chosen for how legibly the readout tears the blades, not for the motor: below about one turn per readout the blades only bend into one swirl, and near two (3590 rpm) they are read so often that the frame fills with evenly stacked pieces that look like a many-bladed fan. A turn and a third per readout is the speed between: two blades stay hooked to the hub with long tapering tails, and one is read twice, torn clean off into fragments floating free at the top and bottom of the disc. It is just under 2397.6 rpm, where the blades pass at exactly 4 x 29.97 Hz, so the torn pattern does not hold still but crawls backwards, a blade pitch about every eight seconds, and the composition visibly turns over while the viewer watches. Drag or scroll up to overdrive it (to 5400 rpm, thinner and more numerous islands), drag down to drop the set speed so the rotor coasts down on its own drag through the hooks and the wagon-wheel speeds, and let go to return it to its notch. The phone is handheld, and its pose is the second thing the readout records. It is a pan across the picture (photo px) and a small roll about the sensor's centre, a mass on the hand's lightly damped spring (2.6 Hz, damping ratio 0.26, the roll on its own 3.1 Hz spring coupled to the sideways pull), simulated at the rotor's own 1/960 s steps and kept in the same history, plus a sway and a physiological tremor (8 to 18 Hz, a few photo px, about a tenth of a degree of a phone's field of view) that is a fixed sum of incommensurate sines of absolute time, so every still is reproducible. Each row of the frame reads the pose at its own instant (the middle of its exposure) and looks into the whole scene through it: the plate, the room, the front guard, the badge and the rotor's disc coordinates are all looked up at the row's posed point, the lamp bands stay on the sensor's rows, and beyond the photo's edge the room runs on as the photo's edge blurred and dimmed. So a pan leans every vertical in the frame by its velocity times the readout, a pan that decelerates bends them, and the blades are read at rotor time plus camera motion, so a flick tears them further or knits them back. Drag sideways to grab the picture (it follows the finger at 0.7, softly limited to 240 photo px) and let go: the phone swings back through rest and rings out over most of a second. ?flick=vx,vy releases the phone from rest at that velocity (photo px/s) as a still's frame starts: ?rpm=2395&t=13.78043&flick=4200,-1200 is the hero mid-swing. The fan head is turned, so the rotor turns in its own tilted plane: an ellipse fitted to the guard rim maps the picture to the disc and back, about a centre on the rim-to-badge axis where the three blade tips reach the same radius (within 1%). The photo is the 3840 px rendition resampled to 2560 px, and the print is cut tight to the fan head, so the guard and blades fill the frame; it is drawn at no more than one photo pixel per device pixel, so the wires stay crisp at DPR 2. It is cut in three by tools/depth/bakes/rolling/bake.py. The plate is the back of the guard and the motor, and the room behind is pulled down to a dim, nearly grey ground (everything that is not steel, keyed by a lightness top-hat and neutrality), the room lit only by the ceiling lamp. The rotor is the three blades as the photo's own transmissive acrylic. Their look comes from the photo, not a fitted field: tools/depth/bakes/rolling/texture.py takes the photo's blade pixels at full detail (the grain, the dust, the rear guard and room seen through the sheet, the real specular) with how far each can be trusted, and acrylic.py unwraps them into each blade's own frame, radius and chord (0 at the leading edge, 1 at the trailing, at that radius), one atlas panel per blade, where a front wire, the paper sticker or the badge hid a blade in the photo, the other two blades' detail at the same radius and chord is laid over its own broad light. The engine computes the same chord for every exposure sub-sample's turned point and reads the atlas there, so the readout shears the photo's real texture into striations along the rows and tears it into photographic fragments: a real photo pulled apart by a real process. The outline is the only thing fitted: the readout shears every row of a turning blade by a different angle, so any burr on its outline would be drawn out into a frayed stroke end, and each blade's outline is refitted in the disc's own plane as a low-order Fourier curve (the greenness edge with the notches the wires and the badge's shadow bit out of it closed, then low-passed along its length), stored as a signed distance field used only to cut and anti-alias the edge over 0.6 device px. The engine draws a bright edge a device px inside the outline, lit by the ceiling lamp as far as the outline's normal (the distance field's gradient, carried through each sub-sample's turn) faces it, so the glint runs round each torn piece as it turns. Each exposure sub-sample composites plate x T + E in linear light, with T = 1 - c + c (1 - A) tint and E = c A body + edge. Inside the disc the rotor sweeps, the plate keeps nothing of the photo (tools/depth/bakes/rolling/reveal.py), so no still, blade-shaped shadow of the photographed blades is left under the torn ones: the dim room continues through, the rear guard is drawn over it (its radial spokes and concentric rings as anti-aliased lines in the rim ellipse's tilted plane, about the point the photo's own spokes converge on, darker than the front and a little out of focus), and the motor housing sits behind the hub, lit from the ceiling lamp. The front guard's wires are cut from the photo itself (tools/depth/bakes/rolling/photo_front.py): a ridge filter steered along their own direction says where a front wire runs (the rear guard's crossing wires and the blades' edges run well off it), and the photo's luminance against the ground beside the wire gives its matte, so each wire is as wide as the photo shows it, keeps the steel's own shading and highlights (unmixed from the green or blue its soft edge caught), crosses over a blade wherever it turns, and runs on out to the rim, where it fades into the same photographed wires the plate keeps instead of ending in mid-air. The spoke count (107), phase, width and colour are measured from the photo's rear-guard steel round the blades, so every gap and every floating fragment shows crisp tinted wires behind clean acrylic. The paper sticker on one blade root is taken out of the acrylic. The front is the steel guard wires and the chrome badge. Over the paper sticker on one blade root the wires are patched from round it. The sheet is 0.74 opaque, so the dim room and the rear guard show through it, tinted green. The badge's slots (an annulus fitted between its rings, everything but the chrome spokes) stay open onto the turning blade roots and the motor behind them. The hero is ?rpm=2395&t=13.78043, the frame the live view opens on (frame 413 of the sensor's clock): two blades hooked to the hub with long tapering tails, one torn off into a fragment at the top and one at the bottom, and the lamp's four bands lying across them, the hand at rest (tremor only). ?rpm=3590&t=0.4 is the old mains speed, nearly two turns per readout. ?rpm=4800&t=0.25 holds the frame (t a multiple of 1/120 s starts the frame at the lamp's trough) that starts at t seconds with the rotor at a steady rpm; ?rpm=1420&t=0.25 is the old desk-fan speed, where the blades only bend. ?scan=degrees sets the readout direction.
sources: Photo: "EF-C30N electric fan which we can understand when SANYO Electrics manufactured (2)" by Tokumeigakarinoaoshima, Wikimedia Commons, CC0 1.0 (public domain dedication). https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:EF-C30N_electric_fan_which_we_can_understand_when_SANYO_Electrics_manufactured_(2).jpg (3840 px rendition, resampled to 2560 px). A SANYO EF-C30N senpuki (logo in use 1976-1986), photographed 2013-06-16. Cropped tight to the fan head, the room behind it graded down to a dim ground, and cut into plate, rotor and front by tools/depth/bakes/rolling/bake.py, with the rear guard behind the blades drawn by tools/depth/bakes/rolling/reveal.py.
